Apostolos
uh-POS-tuh-los
noun
Greek apostolos (αποστολος), “one sent forth, a messenger, an envoy”; from apostellō, to send away with a commission.

Biblical Definition

Apostolos is the Greek word for one sent forth—a messenger, an envoy commissioned and authorized by the one who sends him—and it is the source of the title apostle. In its highest and proper use it names the Twelve whom the Lord Jesus chose and sent, with Paul added as one born out of due time, the authorized eyewitnesses of the risen Christ who laid the foundation of the church and through whom the New Testament Scriptures were given. They were sent with His authority, for he that is sent is not greater than he that sent him; and the church is built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Jesus Christ Himself being the chief corner stone. Remarkably, the word is once applied to Christ Himself: consider the Apostle and High Priest of our profession, Christ Jesus—the One sent by the Father, the great Envoy of God to men. The dictionary holds that the apostolic office, in this foundational sense, was unrepeatable and is now closed: it required being an eyewitness of the risen Lord and bearing His direct commission, and the foundation, once laid, is not laid again. The word may be used in a lower sense of messengers and missionaries sent by the churches, but the office of the apostles of Christ ceased with the apostolic age. The dictionary reads apostolos as the sent one bearing the sender’s authority—supremely the Twelve and Paul, the foundation of the church, and supremely of all, Christ the Apostle of our profession.

Webster 1828 Definition

The Greek word for one sent forth with authority; the title of the Twelve and Paul, foundational eyewitnesses of the risen Christ—an office now closed—and once of Christ Himself, the Apostle of our profession.

APOSTOLOS, Greek for one sent forth, a commissioned messenger.

Names the Twelve and Paul, the authorized eyewitnesses of the risen Christ.

The foundation of the church, Christ Himself the chief corner stone (Eph 2:20).

Once applied to Christ: the Apostle and High Priest of our profession (Heb 3:1).

The foundational office was unrepeatable and is now closed.

Key Scripture

Mat 10:2 — "Now the names of the twelve apostles are these; The first, Simon, who is called Peter, and Andrew his brother; James the son of Zebedee, and John his brother;"

Joh 13:16 — "Verily, verily, I say unto you, The servant is not greater than his lord; neither he that is sent greater than he that sent him."

Heb 3:1 — "Wherefore, holy brethren, partakers of the heavenly calling, consider the Apostle and High Priest of our profession, Christ Jesus;"

Eph 2:20 — "And are built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Jesus Christ himself being the chief corner stone;"

Modern Corruption

The New Apostolic Reformation revives the office of apostle for the present church; the dictionary holds that the foundational apostolic office, requiring eyewitness of the risen Christ, is closed.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The corruption to name is the modern revival of the apostolic office, pressed by the New Apostolic Reformation and kindred movements, which install living “apostles” claiming the authority of the Twelve. But the office of the apostle of Christ, in its proper and foundational sense, was unrepeatable. It required being an eyewitness of the risen Lord and bearing His direct commission—qualifications no man living can meet—and its work was to lay the foundation of the church and to deliver the New Testament Scriptures. A foundation is laid once. To claim apostolic office and authority today is to set a new authority beside the closed canon and to usurp what belonged to the founding age alone.

The principle to recover is the foundational and closed character of the apostolate, and the supremacy of Christ the great Apostle. The church is built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, with Christ the chief corner stone; that foundation, once laid, abides but is not re-laid. The word apostolos may still describe a messenger sent by the churches, but the office of the apostles of Christ ceased with them. And above all stands the Apostle of our profession, the Son sent by the Father, whose authority the apostles bore and to whom the church looks, having their testimony in the Scripture they left.
